captions: Hello, and welcome to Atomic English, Stage 8. In this lesson: The lighthouse.
Analyse how sentence length and structure create suspense.
Here are some new words. Suspense. A feeling of excitement or worry about what will happen. Foreshadow.
Give a hint of something that will happen later. Ominous. Suggesting that something bad is going to happen.
And some more words. Flicker. Shine unsteadily, on and off. Dread.
Great fear of something that is going to happen. Isolated. Far away from other people or places.
Time for a question. The video will stop.
Which word means: a feeling of excitement or worry about what will happen?
Now some grammar: Sentence variety for effect.
Long sentences can build atmosphere; very short sentences create shock or tension.
A one-word sentence can stop the reader. For example: The waves crashed against the rocks,
the wind screamed through every gap in the old stone walls, and the lamp swung wildly above her head.
Then silence. Nothing.
Now listen, and read along. The lighthouse. The lighthouse stood on an isolated rock,
three kilometres from the coast, and for forty years nobody had lived there.
That was why Mira had been surprised when her uncle offered to take her out in his boat to see it.
By the time they reached the rock, ominous grey clouds had covered the sun. The wind was rising.
Her uncle tied the boat to an iron ring and handed her a torch. ‘Ten minutes,’ he said.
‘Then we go back.’ Inside, the spiral staircase climbed into darkness.
Mira counted the steps as she went up: twenty, fifty, ninety.
At the top, the great lamp was cold and dusty, exactly as she had expected.
Then she heard it. Footsteps. Slow, heavy footsteps, climbing the stairs below her.
She leaned over the rail and shone her torch down. The beam flickered. The staircase was empty.
Another question. The video will stop. How long had the lighthouse been empty?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like suspense, foreshadow, ominous.
You practised sentence variety for effect. And you read The lighthouse. Now try the practice questions.
See you next time!

captions: Hello, and welcome to Atomic English, Stage 8. In this lesson: It must have been the wind.
Use past modal verbs (must have, might have, can't have, should have) to speculate about the past.
Here are some new words. Speculate. Guess about something without being sure. Explanation.
A reason that makes something clear. Rational. Based on clear thinking, not feelings.
And some more words. Imagination. The ability to create pictures and ideas in your mind. Echo.
A sound that is repeated as it bounces back. Reassure. Say something to make someone less worried.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: guess about something without being sure?
Now some grammar: Past modals of deduction. Must have plus past participle means almost certain.
Might have or could have means possible. Can't have means almost certainly not.
Should have means it was the right thing, but it didn't happen. For example: It must have been the wind.
For example: She might have heard an echo. For example: He can't have seen a ghost.
For example: We should have left earlier.
Now listen, and read along. What happened in the lighthouse? When Mira ran back to the boat, she was shaking.
‘Someone was on the stairs,’ she said. ‘I heard them.’ Her uncle listened carefully.
‘It can't have been a person,’ he said. ‘I was standing by the only door the whole time,
and nobody went in after you.’ ‘Then what was it?’ ‘It might have been the echo of your own footsteps.
Those old stone walls can play tricks.
Or it could have been loose metal moving in the wind.’ Mira wasn't sure.
The sound must have come from somewhere – and it had seemed so real.
‘I should have warned you,’ her uncle admitted. ‘Old buildings make strange noises.
But your imagination is a powerful thing.’ He smiled to reassure her, but as they sailed away,
Mira noticed he didn't look back at the lighthouse once.
Another question. The video will stop. Why does the uncle think it can't have been a person?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like speculate, explanation, rational.
You practised past modals of deduction. And you read What happened in the lighthouse?
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

‘It might have been the echo of your own footsteps. Those old stone walls can play tricks. Or it could have been loose metal moving in the wind.’
Mira wasn't sure. The sound must have come from somewhere – and it had seemed so real.
‘I should have warned you,’ her uncle admitted. ‘Old buildings make strange noises. But your imagination is a powerful thing.’ He smiled to reassure her, but as they sailed away, Mira noticed he didn't look back at the lighthouse once.

A.prompt: Read “The lighthouse”. Why is ‘Then she heard it.’ in its own paragraph?
A.ctx:
The lighthouse
The lighthouse stood on an isolated rock, three kilometres from the coast, and for forty years nobody had lived there. That was why Mira had been surprised when her uncle offered to take her out in his boat to see it.
By the time they reached the rock, ominous grey clouds had covered the sun. The wind was rising. Her uncle tied the boat to an iron ring and handed her a torch.
‘Ten minutes,’ he said. ‘Then we go back.’
Inside, the spiral staircase climbed into darkness. Mira counted the steps as she went up: twenty, fifty, ninety. At the top, the great lamp was cold and dusty, exactly as she had expected.
Then she heard it.
Footsteps. Slow, heavy footsteps, climbing the stairs below her.
She leaned over the rail and shone her torch down. The beam flickered. The staircase was empty.
